content:
The United States has charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses in what the Justice Department on Tuesday described as the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in its history, an eight-month crackdown that reached from American courtrooms to fraud compounds on four continents.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the results at a press conference in Washington alongside FBI Director Kash Patel, saying prosecutors had filed more than 400 criminal cases across 85 federal districts since President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud targeting Americans. The actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and prison sentences, according to the [Justice Department](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-largest-ever-crackdown-scammers-targeting-over-800-defendants).

"We are not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long."

The figures behind the announcement show the scale of the problem the government says it is confronting. The Justice Department said one in ten Americans has fallen victim to a scam this year, and the cases brought since March span almost every kind of fraud now aimed at American households: fake jury-duty fines, sweepstakes schemes targeting elderly victims, timeshare fraud in Mexico allegedly run by drug cartels, and websites impersonating federal courts.

One case illustrates how ordinary the deception can be. In Georgia, prosecutors charged 14 people in three indictments after members of prison gangs allegedly used smuggled mobile phones and handwritten scripts to call victims and tell them they had missed jury duty and would be arrested unless they paid a fine immediately. A further 17 defendants were charged in state court over the smuggling of the phones themselves.

The most striking part of the crackdown, however, took place overseas. Under an FBI initiative called Operation Blackout, agents working with law enforcement in more than 10 countries raided the industrial-scale fraud compounds where many of these scams are run. Patel said the operation had seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, confiscated more than 14,000 digital devices and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents.

Those compounds function almost as towns, Patel said — self-contained sites where criminal networks force human trafficking victims to run online fraud schemes against Americans thousands of miles away. The joint operations have freed more than 2,200 trafficked workers, according to the FBI.

"They thought they could get away with it in Southeast Asia. They moved to Africa. They moved to the Middle East," Patel said. "We annihilated them on every single continent that they chose to operate and attack American citizens."

The global reach of the networks was underlined by a separate enforcement push coordinated in London, which led to 28 arrests across Africa, $11 million in seized assets, the rescue of 120 trafficked workers and the removal of 3.7 million fraudulent Facebook and Instagram accounts. Jeanine Pirro, the US Attorney for the District of Columbia, said strike-force teams had broken up Chinese organised crime affiliates operating in Cambodia, Laos and Burma that were "rapidly expanding around the globe."

The crackdown was coordinated by the Justice Department's Criminal Division, which assembled a dedicated team of prosecutors to identify scammers, disrupt their networks and hold them accountable. It drew in agencies across the government, including the FBI, the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Secret Service, the Treasury Department, the Postal Inspection Service, the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

The two headline numbers in the announcement measure different things, and the distinction matters. The $8 billion figure is the value of intended victim losses recovered or prevented through the Justice Department's cases — money prosecutors say would otherwise have been stolen from Americans. The nearly $17 billion cited by the FBI is the value of illicit funds seized in the global Operation Blackout raids, which includes criminal proceeds held by the networks themselves. Both figures dwarf the sums in any previous American anti-fraud operation.

What the announcement did not answer is how much of the recovered money will actually reach victims. Prosecutors said the cases include charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and sentences, but they gave no breakdown of how many of the more than 800 defendants have been convicted, how many remain at large overseas, or how restitution to victims will be handled. The Justice Department also did not say whether the dismantled compounds have stayed closed, a question that matters because scam networks have repeatedly reopened in new locations after raids in Southeast Asia.

The crackdown comes as online and phone fraud continues to hit American households at staggering rates, and as the fraud economy itself becomes more industrialised. The compounds raided under Operation Blackout are not small call centres but organised operations that combine human trafficking with large-scale digital fraud, using trafficked workers to run romance scams, fake investment schemes and impersonation frauds against victims they never meet. The FBI said it had directly warned more than 11,000 Americans that they were being targeted, preventing more than $690 million in potential losses.

The surge also reflects a shift in how the United States treats fraud: not as a collection of individual crimes but as an organised, transnational industry. The executive order that launched it in March directed agencies across the government to treat scam networks as a single problem, and the involvement of the Treasury, the communications regulator and the markets regulator alongside the FBI and the Justice Department suggests the government now sees fraud as a financial, technological and diplomatic challenge at once.

For Americans, the practical advice from officials remains unchanged: government agencies do not demand payment by phone, no legitimate court fines are collected through gift cards or wire transfers, and anyone contacted out of the blue about a missed jury duty or an unpaid fine should hang up and call the court directly. The Justice Department said it would use "every tool at its disposal" to disrupt the schemes, but the scale of the fraud — one victim in ten this year — means the crackdown's real test will be whether the networks stay dismantled once the press conference is over.

The operation arrives in a month already crowded with major cybercrime news, from the [breach that exposed customers' card numbers and CVV codes at software platform Cleverbridge](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/cleverbridge-breach-card-numbers-cvv-stolen-november-2026) to the [accounting probe that sent Nvidia shares plunging](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/sec-probes-nvidia-accounting-shares-plunge-november-2026). What sets the anti-scam surge apart is its scope: it is the first time the United States has treated online fraud as a global enforcement campaign, with raids, arrests and asset seizures coordinated across continents rather than prosecutions confined to American courts.
summary: The Justice Department has charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses in the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in American history, while the FBI's Operation Blackout dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents and freed more than 2,200 human trafficking victims forced to run the frauds.
title: US charges more than 800 people in largest anti-scam crackdown in history, dismantling 29 fraud compounds on four continents
